title: Renter Friendly Apartment Upgrades That Won't Cost Your Deposit
meta_description: Renter friendly apartment upgrades you can undo at move-out: lighting, walls, hardware, storage and floors, and how to remove each one.
body_html:
A rental doesn't have to feel like a rental. With the right renter friendly apartment upgrades, you can fix bad lighting, dated hardware and blank walls, then put everything back the way you found it when you move out. Here's what works, what to watch out for and how to get your deposit back.

Start with your lease and a parts box

Before you change anything, reread your lease. Some leases ban nail holes, painting or swapping fixtures. Others allow small changes as long as you restore them. If something isn't clear, email your landlord or property manager and ask. A written "yes" protects you far better than a verbal one.

Next, grab a shoebox or plastic bin and label it "Original parts." Every cabinet pull, shower head, light shade and screw you remove goes in a labeled zip-top bag inside that box. Take a quick photo of each item installed before you remove it. At move-out, you'll know exactly what goes where.

Also take date-stamped photos of every room on move-in day. If there's a question about damage later, you'll have proof of what was already there.

Fix the lighting first

Harsh overhead lights make any space feel like an office. Lighting is the upgrade that changes the feel of a room fastest, and most of it needs zero tools.

  • Plug-in wall sconces. They mount with a couple of small screws or strong removable adhesive and plug into an outlet. Use a cord cover painted to match the wall to hide the cord.
  • Warm bulbs. Swap cool bulbs for warm white (around 2700K). Keep the originals in your parts box.
  • Smart bulbs. Dimmable smart bulbs let you set scenes without touching the wiring. We cover more options in our guide to smart home gadgets for apartments.
  • Battery puck lights. Stick them under kitchen cabinets or inside dark closets for instant task lighting.
  • Floor and table lamps. Layering two or three lamps at different heights beats one bright ceiling fixture every time.

Update walls without paint

If painting is off the table, you still have options.

Peel-and-stick wallpaper

Removable wallpaper works best on smooth walls with eggshell or satin paint. Flat paint and freshly painted walls are riskier because the adhesive can pull paint off when you remove it. Always test a small piece in a hidden spot, like inside a closet, and leave it for a week or two before committing. Start with one accent wall so removal stays manageable.

Hang art the low-damage way

Removable adhesive hooks and picture-hanging strips hold lightweight frames well. Follow the weight rating on the package and clean the wall with rubbing alcohol first so the adhesive grips. For heavier pieces, a picture ledge or a large framed mirror leaned against the wall gives you the look without any holes.

If your lease allows small nail holes, those are often easier to patch than adhesive damage. A small tub of spackle and a putty knife fix them in minutes before move-out.

Swap hardware and fixtures (with permission)

Cheap builder-grade hardware is one of the easiest things to upgrade. These swaps usually need only a screwdriver or wrench:

  • Cabinet knobs and pulls. Measure the distance between screw holes on existing pulls so new ones fit without drilling. Many come in standard sizes like 3 or 3.75 inches.
  • Shower head. Most unscrew by hand or with a wrench. Wrap plumber's tape around the threads to prevent leaks.
  • Light fixture shades. Many ceiling fixtures have a glass shade you can swap without touching wiring.
  • Toilet seat. Two bolts and you're done.

Anything involving wiring, like replacing a ceiling fixture, should go through your landlord. Even if you're handy, an electrical change in a rental can raise liability and insurance questions. Ask first, and if they agree, consider having maintenance or a licensed electrician do it.

Upgrade the kitchen and bathroom

These rooms take the most wear and usually have the most dated finishes.

  • Peel-and-stick backsplash tiles cover a plain wall behind the sink or counter. Check the product's heat guidance before putting any near the stove.
  • Removable contact paper can refresh shelf liners or cover worn drawer bottoms.
  • A rolling cart or freestanding shelf adds storage without drilling into anything.
  • Over-the-toilet shelving turns wasted wall space into bathroom storage.
  • A new shower curtain hung high on a tension rod makes a small bathroom look taller.

For more kitchen-specific ideas, see our guide to small kitchen organization ideas.

Cover floors and dress up windows

You can't rip out stained carpet or worn vinyl, but you can cover it. A large area rug grounds a room and hides a lot. Put a rug pad underneath so it doesn't slide or scratch hardwood.

For windows, landlord blinds are often the first thing that makes a rental look like a rental. Options that don't require new hardware:

  • Tension rods inside the window frame for lightweight curtains or café panels.
  • Removable frosted window film for privacy in bathrooms or street-facing rooms. It clings with water and peels off.
  • Curtains hung high and wide. If you can install a curtain rod, mounting it closer to the ceiling makes windows look larger. Rod brackets leave a few small holes, so check your lease first.

Quick reference: popular upgrades and how to undo them

UpgradeDeposit riskHow to undo it
Warm or smart bulbsNoneReinstall original bulbs
Removable adhesive hooksLowPull the release tab slowly, straight down along the wall
Peel-and-stick wallpaperLow to mediumWarm with a hair dryer and peel slowly at a low angle
Cabinet hardwareLowReinstall originals from your parts box
Shower headLowUnscrew and reinstall the original with fresh plumber's tape
Window filmLowPeel from a corner and wipe off residue
Curtain rod bracketsMediumRemove, then patch holes with spackle and touch-up paint if allowed

Your move-out checklist

  1. Pull out your parts box and reinstall every original fixture, pull and bulb.
  2. Remove adhesive products slowly. Use a hair dryer on low to soften stubborn adhesive.
  3. Wipe off any residue with a little rubbing alcohol or an adhesive remover safe for painted surfaces. Test it in a hidden spot first.
  4. Patch small holes with spackle, let it dry, and sand lightly.
  5. Compare each room to your move-in photos.

Making a rental feel like yours also matters for how you feel at home. We dig into that in the psychology of decorating a rental.

Frequently asked questions

Will peel-and-stick wallpaper damage my walls?

It can if your walls have flat paint or were painted recently. Test a small piece in a hidden spot for a week or two, and remove it slowly with gentle heat from a hair dryer.

Can I change light fixtures in an apartment?

Only with your landlord's permission, since it involves wiring. Plug-in sconces, lamps and smart bulbs give you better lighting without touching the electrical system.

Do I need to reinstall the original cabinet hardware when I move out?

Usually, yes, unless your landlord agrees in writing to keep your upgrade. Store the originals in a labeled bag so reinstalling takes minutes.

Are removable adhesive hooks really damage-free?

They're low-risk when used correctly. Clean the wall first, respect the weight limit and pull the release tab straight down along the wall rather than out toward you.

Made your rental feel like home without losing your deposit? Post a before-and-after photo of your setup in our Small-Space Living community and show other renters what worked for you.
